Azure Cloud-Native Platform Updates

Follow meaningful documentation updates across Microsoft's Azure cloud-native platform, spanning container orchestration and fleet management (AKS, AKS Automatic, Application Network, AKS Support, AKS Arc, Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes, and Kubernetes Fleet Manager), container registry (Azure Container Registry), application networking (Application Gateway for Containers), and Azure Linux. The tracker also summarizes the latest five AKS and Application Network releases.

It automatically scans for changes, then uses AI to summarize and highlight updates that are most likely to matter — such as new features, deprecations, and significant content revisions.

Minor edits (like typos, formatting tweaks, and other low-impact changes) are usually filtered out. Because the process is automated, some updates may be missed or summaries may not capture every nuance.

For complete accuracy, you can always follow the provided links to the original Microsoft documentation.

With this tracker, you can:

  • Quickly scan meaningful AKS, AKS Automatic, AKS Support, App Net, Arc K8s, AKS Arc, Azure Linux, ACR, AGC, and Fleet documentation changes from the past 7 days
  • Stay up to date with the latest AKS and App Net release notes without digging through every doc page
  • Search and browse CVE security data across AKS releases and VHD node images, powered by the AKS Vulnerability Data API (Public Preview)

Get the Latest AKS Docs - Every Week, in Your Inbox

Release 2026-10-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-27

The release on 2026-10-25 introduces automatic upgrades for unsupported Kubernetes versions and updates to node pools.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will automatically upgrade unsupported clusters after a grace period.
  • Default OS SKU for node pools changes to Ubuntu 26.04 with Kubernetes 1.38.
🔑

Key Features

  • Kubernetes 1.37 is now generally available as Long-Term Support.
  • Node Auto Provisioning (NAP) enhancements include new CRDs and features.
💡

Good to Know

  • Review upgrade channels to prepare for automated upgrades.
  • Community support for Kubernetes 1.34 ends by November 2026.

Release Notes 2026-09-25

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-10-01

The 2026-09-25 release introduces significant updates and deprecations. Key features include the general availability of identity bindings and preview support for Ubuntu 26.04.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • Windows Server 2022 is not supported in Kubernetes version 1.37 and above.
  • Flatcar Container Linux node images are removed, affecting scaling operations.
  • The annotation service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-pip-tags no longer overrides public IP tags.
🔑

Key Features

  • Identity bindings are now generally available.
  • Ubuntu 26.04 is available in preview.
  • Windows Server OS SKU migration to 2025 is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • AKS will auto-migrate deprecated Availability Sets clusters after September 30, 2026.
  • AKS release order has been updated for Central US and East US.
  • Check AKS Release Tracker for detailed release timing.

Release 2026-09-04

AKS
View Release
📅 2026-09-09

This release introduces Kubernetes 1.37 and autoscaling for VM node pools. It also announces the retirement of Azure Linux with OS Guard.

❌

Breaking Changes

  • AKS will remove Azure Linux with OS Guard node images on March 10, 2027.
  • AKS no longer produces VHDs for Windows Server 2019 and version 23H2.
🔑

Key Features

  • Autoscaling for Virtual Machines node pools is now generally available.
  • Kubernetes patch versions 1.36.3, 1.35.7, and 1.34.10 are available.
  • On-Demand Monitor for node health checks is in preview.
💡

Good to Know

  • LocalDNS is enabled automatically for compatible cluster networking.
  • AKS rejects updates that remove IPv6 from dual-stack clusters.
  • Managed namespace creation rejects names starting with reserved prefixes.

Support for Azure Linux with OS Guard in Azure Kubernetes Service will end on December 10, 2026. Azure Container Linux is the replacement for Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview). Starting on December 10, 2026: - Users won’t be able to create new Azure Linux with OS Guard (preview) node pools. - AKS won’t produce new node images for affected node pools. - Existing node pools won’t receive security patches. On March 10, 2027, AKS will remove the Azure Linux with OS Guard node images. After the images are removed, scaling and remediation operations, including reimage and redeploy operations, will fail for affected node pools. You can use either of the following migration options: - Migrate an existing Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool in place by following the Migrate nodes to Azure Container Linux for Azure Kubernetes Service documentation. This operation preforms a standard node image upgrade. - Alternatively, create a new Azure Container Linux node pool, migrate and validate workloads, and then delete the Azure Linux with OS Guard node pool. Follow Add Azure Container Linux node pools and remove existing node pools. For other available options, see the AKS node operating system. If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A or AKS GitHub Repository. If you have a support plan and need technical help, create a support request.

Ubuntu 20.04 has been replaced by newer supported versions, including Ubuntu 22.04 and Ubuntu 24.04. We encourage you to transition to Ubuntu 22.04+ before the retirement date. Required action: If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with a Confidential VM (CVM) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.33+ where Ubuntu 24.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for CVM workloads. If you’re currently using Ubuntu 20.04 with Federal Information Process Standard (FIPS) on AKS, follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ where Ubuntu 22.04 will be the default Ubuntu version for FIPS workloads. To avoid service disruptions, scaling restrictions, and remain supported, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.34+ by March 17, 2027. On March 31, 2027 Azure Monitor will be deprecating the sidecar for remote-write of Prometheus metrics to Azure Monitor Workspace. This is as part of our ongoing efforts to improve reliability and reduce complexity. We recommend configuring your self-hosted Prometheus or Prometheus Operator to remote-write directly to Azure Monitor Workspace. All authentication methods are supported in the Prometheus remote-write configuration, and direct remote-write is fully compatible with the Prometheus Operator. You can find detailed configuration guidance in the official documentation. This approach removes the need for the sidecar and simplifies your setup. We encourage you to transition to direct Prometheus remote-write as soon as possible to take advantage of the improved experience and ensure uninterrupted service. If you have any questions or need assistance during this transition, please feel free to contact ciprometheus@microsoft.com with your name, company name, email contact and subscription IDs.

On June 30, 2027, we'll retire Ubuntu 22.04 on Azure Kubernetes Service. To avoid disruptions, transition to Ubuntu 24.04 or later by that date. Newer supported versions include kernel updates and security improvements. Until June 30, 2027, you can continue to use Ubuntu 22.04 on AKS without disruption. If you don't migrate by June 30, 2027, you won't be able to create new node pools, AKS won't produce new node images, and you'll no longer receive security patches for existing node pools. On April 30, 2028 AKS will remove Ubuntu 22.04 node images and existing code, causing scaling and remediation operations to fail. Migration Options: - Default Operating System SKU (OSSku): If you're using 'Ubuntu,' you'll automatically migrate to Ubuntu 24.04 when you upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.35 or later. - Versioned OSSku: If you're using 'Ubuntu2204,' update your OSSku to 'Ubuntu' for Kubernetes 1.35 or later, or 'Ubuntu2404' for Kubernetes 1.32 or later. Read moreRead less
Beginning September 30, 2027, support for the pod name dimension on the following Azure Monitor platform metrics is retiring, and these metrics are transitioning to aggregate pod counters: - Number of pods by phase (kube_pod_status_phase) - Number of pods in Ready state (kube_pod_status_ready) After this change: - Metric names remain unchanged. - Aggregate pod counts remain available. - Namespace-level monitoring scenarios remain supported. - The pod name dimension will no longer be available for filtering, grouping, or alerting. During the deprecation period, AKS will maintain both the existing and the new aggregate implementations. Both are populated with data, existing monitoring experiences will continue to function, and you will have at least one year of historical data in the aggregate implementation before retirement. You may be affected if any dashboard, workbook, alert, automation, or monitoring workflow: - Uses kube_pod_status_phase or kube_pod_status_ready and filters on the pod name dimension. - Splits or groups results by the pod name dimension. Recommended action: - If you use aggregate pod counts, no action is required. - If you use the pod name dimension, update dashboards, alerts, workbooks, and automation before September 30, 2027. For pod-level monitoring and troubleshooting, we recommend using Azure Monitor Managed Prometheus and Kubernetes-native pod metrics. Help and support If you have questions, get answers from community experts in Microsoft Q&A.

Read moreRead less
The Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension for Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes will be retired on October 9, 2027. Customers currently using the extension should plan to migrate to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension before the retirement date. The Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension provides equivalent functionality for accessing and synchronizing secrets from Azure Key Vault for workloads running on Azure Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters. In addition, the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension includes enhancements such as support for offline access to secrets and authentication using workload identity federation, enabling applications to access Azure Key Vault without storing long-lived credentials on the cluster. After retirement, the Azure Key Vault Secrets Provider Extension will no longer receive new features, bug fixes, security updates, or technical support. Migration guidance is available to help customers transition their workloads and configurations to the Azure Key Vault Secret Store Extension ahead of retirement.

Azure Container Registry (ACR) implements Docker Content Trust (DCT), allowing image publishers to sign their images and image consumers to verify that the images they pull are signed. With advancements in technology, Docker Content Trust no longer meets the requirements of modern supply chain security for containers. As a result, Docker Content Trust will be deprecated and no longer available in ACR after March 31, 2028. If you currently use Docker Content Trust, you should transition to the Notary Project ecosystem, including their open-source supply chain tool, Notation. How does this affect me? - Starting September 30, 2025, customers will no longer be able to enable Docker Content Trust on Azure Container Registry. - Data stored in Azure Container Registry for signing and verifying signatures with Docker Content Trust will be permanently deleted on March 31, 2028. - Docker Content Trust function will be completely removed from Azure Container Registry on March 31, 2028. Required Action Start your transition to Notary Project today and enhance the security and trust of your container ecosystem. Use the following articles to get started. Signing: - Use AKV with self-signed certificates - Use AKV with CA-issued certificates - Sign in ADO pipelines - Sign in GitHub workflows Verification: - Verify in ADO pipelines - Verify in GitHub workflows - Verify on AKS

Read moreRead less
Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS will be retired on November 30, 2025, please transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by that date. Azure Linux 2.0 has been replaced by the newer supported version Azure Linux 3.0. We encourage you to transition to Azure Linux 3.0 prior to the retirement date to experience the capabilities of Azure Linux 3.0 including kernel updates and security improvements. From now to November 30, 2025, you can continue to use Azure Linux 2.0 without disruption. On November 30, 2025, Azure Linux 2.0 will no longer be supported on AKS; AKS will no longer create new node pools, produce new node images, or provide security updates for Azure Linux 2.0 after that date. On March 31, 2026, Azure Linux 2.0 node images will be removed. This will cause scaling operations to fail. Customers can transition to Azure Linux 3.0 by taking one of the following actions: - If you’re currently using Azure Linux 2.0 on AKS, please follow our instructions to upgrade your Kubernetes version to 1.32+. - Alternately, starting Kubernetes version 1.28+ you can perform an in-place node pool update from --os-sku AzureLinux to --os-sku AzureLinux3, enabling you to migrate existing node pools from Azure Linux 2.0 to 3.0 while remaining on the same k8s version. Your node pool will automatically reimage to the equivalent Azure Linux 3.0 node image. See documentation here. To avoid service disruptions, please follow our instructions to migrate to Azure Linux 3.0 by November 30, 2025.

                                  @@ -1,14 +1,14 @@-# Increased memory usage reported in Kubernetes 1.25 or later versions - Azure | Microsoft Learn+# Increased memory usage reported in Kubernetes 1.25 or later versions in AKS - Azure | Microsoft Learn  ## Summary -This article discusses how to resolve an *increased reported memory usage* issue in Microsoft Azure Kubernetes 1.25 or a later version.+This article discusses how to resolve an increased reported memory usage issue in Microsoft Azure Kubernetes 1.25 or a later version.  ## Symptoms  You experience one or more of the following symptoms: -- Pods report increased memory usage after you upgrade a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster to Kubernetes 1.25 or a later version.+- Pods report increased memory usage after you upgrade an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster to Kubernetes 1.25 or a later version. - A node reports memory usage that's greater than in earlier versions of Kubernetes when you run the [kubectl top node](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubectl/kubectl-commands#-em-node-em-) command. - Increased pod evictions and memory pressure occur within a node. @@ -22,21 +22,17 @@ This issue is distinct from the memory saturation in nodes that's caused by appl  ## Solution +The following solutions can help mitigate the increased memory usage issue:+ - If you observe frequent memory pressure on the nodes, upgrade your subscription to increase the amount of memory that's available to your virtual machines (VMs). - If you see a higher eviction rate on the pods, [use higher limits and requests for pods](/en-us/azure/aks/developer-best-practices-resource-management#define-pod-resource-requests-and-limits).-- `cgroup` v2 uses a different API than `cgroup` v1. If there are any applications that directly access the `cgroup` file system, update them to later versions that support `cgroup` v2. For example:--    - **Third-party monitoring and security agents**:--        Some monitoring and security agents depend on the `cgroup` file system. Update these agents to versions that support `cgroup` v2.-    - **Java applications**:--        Use versions that fully support `cgroup` v2:-+- `cgroup` v2 uses a different API than `cgroup` v1. If there are any applications that directly access the `cgroup` file system, update them to later versions that support `cgroup`v2. The following are examples:+    - **Third-party monitoring and security agents** Some monitoring and security agents depend on the `cgroup` file system. Update these agents to versions that support `cgroup` v2.+    - **Java applications** Use versions that fully support `cgroup`v2, like the following:         - OpenJDK/HotSpot: `jdk8u372`, `11.0.16`, `15`, and later versions.         - IBM Semeru Runtimes: `8.0.382.0`, `11.0.20.0`, `17.0.8.0`, and later versions.         - IBM Java: `8.0.8.6` and later versions.-    - **uber-go/automaxprocs**: If you're using the `uber-go/automaxprocs` package, ensure the version is `v1.5.1` or later.+    - **uber-go/automaxprocs** If you're using the `uber-go/automaxprocs` package, ensure the version is `v1.5.1` or later. - An alternative temporary solution is to revert the `cgroup` version on your nodes by using the DaemonSet. Important@@ -47,7 +43,7 @@ Important  Note -If you experience only an increase in memory use without any of the other symptoms that are mentioned in the "Symptoms" section, you don't have to take any action.+If you experience only an increase in memory use without any of the other symptoms that are mentioned in the Symptoms section, you don't have to take any action.  ## Status @@ -55,7 +51,7 @@ We're actively working with the Kubernetes community to resolve the underlying i  As part of the resolution, we plan to adjust the eviction thresholds or update [resource reservations](/en-us/azure/aks/concepts-clusters-workloads#resource-reservations), depending on the outcome of the fix. -## Reference+## References  - [Node memory usage on cgroupv2 reported higher than cgroupv1](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/118916) (GitHub issue)

                                    @@ -1,8 +1,8 @@-# Troubleshoot the K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError error code (51) - Azure | Microsoft Learn+# Troubleshoot K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError error code (51) in AKS - Azure | Microsoft Learn  ## Summary -This article describes how to identify and resolve the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error (also known as error code `ERR_K8S_API_SERVER_CONN_FAIL`, error number 51). This error might occur when you create, start, scale, or upgrade a Microsoft Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster or node pool.+This article helps you troubleshoot the `K8SAPIServerConnFailVMExtensionError` error code (also known as `ERR_K8S_API_SERVER_CONN_FAIL`, error number 51) so that you can successfully create, start, scale, or upgrade an Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) cluster or node pool.  When AKS provisions a Linux node, the node bootstrap script (delivered through the `vmssCSE` Custom Script Extension) checks whether the node can reach the cluster's Kubernetes API server on TCP port 443 before it starts the kubelet. If the node can resolve the API server address but can't establish a connection to it, the script exits with code 51, the node isn't registered in the cluster, and the operation fails.

In this article, we introduce key concepts for cross-cluster networking for Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager. -Important--Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager preview features are available on a self-service, opt-in basis. Deploy the application using the `kubectl apply` command and specify the name of your YAML manifest.+### Validate the MIG profiles configuration -    ```azurecli-    kubectl apply -f mixed-strategy-example.yaml-    ```-3. Verify the allocated GPU devices using the `kubectl exec` command. This command returns a list of the cluster nodes.+- Supply exactly one profile value to `--gpu-mig-profiles` for `Single`, not repeated entries to specify a partition count.+- Don't also supply `--gpu-instance-profile` flag. You can't combine `--gpu-instance-profile` and `--gpu-mig-profiles` on the same MIG node pool.++The `--gpu-instance-profile` flag remains supported for the single strategy, and AKS doesn't automatically convert it to `--gpu-mig-profiles`. To verify a new node pool created with `--gpu-mig-strategy` and `--gpu-mig-profiles`, run `az aks nodepool show` and check `gpuProfile.nvidia.migStrategy` and `gpuProfile.nvidia.migProfiles`.++## Migrate to use the managed MIG profiles++1. Inventory the current pool's VM size, `gpuInstanceProfile`, node image, and advertised partition capacity. Record workload selectors, affinity, taints, tolerations, and GPU requests. Check whether the existing NVIDIA device plugin or GPU operator serves other node pools.+2. Ensure that your self-managed NVIDIA device plugin and any GPU operator don't reconcile the replacement MIG pool's nodes. Adjust their node targeting by using the supported configuration for your installation.+3. Create a replacement MIG node pool with a distinct name. For example, to preserve a `MIG3g` layout on `Standard_NC24ads_A100_v4`, use the following command. Substitute the supported SKU and single profile that matches your migration plan. Don't pass `--gpu-instance-profile`.      ```azurecli-    kubectl exec nvidia-mixed -- nvidia-smi -L+    az aks nodepool add \+      --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" \+      --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" \+      --name migreplacement \+      --node-vm-size Standard_NC24ads_A100_v4 \+      --enable-managed-gpu=true \+      --gpu-mig-strategy Single \+      --gpu-mig-profiles MIG3g \+      --node-count 1     ```+4. Run the configuration, readiness, capacity, and workload checks in this article against `migreplacement`. Update the sample selector to `agentpool: migreplacement`. Confirm the expected partition size and device access before moving application workloads.+5. Move workloads gradually by updating pool selectors or affinity and any required tolerations. Single-strategy workloads continue to request `nvidia.com/gpu`. Verify application behavior, throughput, latency, and memory usage on the replacement pool.+6. After verifying the replacement, drain or retire workloads on the old node pool and delete it. Keep the old pool available until your migration validation is complete when capacity permits. Remove the self-managed NVIDIA device plugin installation only after confirming that no remaining pools need it. -    The following example resembles output showing successfully created deployments and services:+## Troubleshoot and remove the node pool -    ```output-    GPU 0: NVIDIA A100 40GB PCIe (UUID: GPU-48aeb943-9458-4282-da24-e5f49e0db44b)-    MIG 1g.5gb     Device  0: (UUID: MIG-fb42055e-9e53-5764-9278-438605a3014c)-    ```+### Troubleshoot scheduling and partition advertisement -Important+A pod that requests more `nvidia.com/gpu` resources than the eligible nodes can provide remains pending with an insufficient-resource scheduling event. Inspect its status and events:++```bash+kubectl describe pod nvidia-single+```++If nodes don't advertise partitions, inspect node conditions, managed settings, and the selected image and profile. Don't install a second plugin or patch AKS-managed components as a workaround.++The following errors can occur when you create the node pool:++| Error code | Cause | Resolution |+| --- | --- | --- |+| `MIGNotSupportedForVMSize` | The VM size doesn't support MIG. | Use a supported MIG-capable GPU VM size. |+| `InvalidOrNoneMIGProfile` | The profile is invalid, or you specified `None`. | Specify exactly one valid MIG profile for the VM size. |+| `MIGProfilesNodeImageNotSupported` | The AKS node image is older than the minimum supported version. | Use a node image version of `202609.01.0` or later. |++Azure CLI might show `BadRequest` as the top-level code, so also read the validation message.++### Delete the sample pod and MIG node pool++Delete the sample pod:++```bash+kubectl delete pod nvidia-single --ignore-not-found=true+```++Before deleting a node pool that runs other workloads, create replacement capacity, migrate the workloads, and verify application health. Then remove the node pool:++```azurecli+az aks nodepool delete \+  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" \+  --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" \+  --name "$SINGLE_POOL"+```++Verify that the MIG node pool is removed: -The `latest` tag for CUDA images has been deprecated on Docker Hub. Please refer to [NVIDIA's repository](https://hub.docker.com/r/nvidia/cuda/tags) for the latest images and corresponding tags.+```azurecli+az aks nodepool list \+  --resource-group "$RESOURCE_GROUP" \+  --cluster-name "$CLUSTER_NAME" \+  --query "[?name=='$SINGLE_POOL'].name" --output json+``` -## Troubleshooting+The output should be `[]`. Confirm that no Kubernetes nodes remain for the pool: -If you don't see multi-instance GPU capability after creating the node pool, confirm the API version isn't older than *2021-08-01*.+```bash+kubectl get nodes -l agentpool="$SINGLE_POOL"+```

                                                  @@ -1,15 +1,13 @@ # Use scheduled start gates in Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager Update Run Strategies | Microsoft Learn +**Applies to:** ✔️ Fleet Manager ✔️ Fleet Manager with hub cluster+ Platform administrators often need to ensure that cluster updates only start at specific days and times. For example, choose times when teams are available to monitor or when user traffic is at its lowest.  Fleet Manager provides scheduled start gates that platform administrators can use to delay the progression of an update run until a specified day and time. For example, you can place a scheduled start gate before the production stage of an update strategy. This gate ensures that production clusters don't begin updating until the scheduled time, even if earlier stages complete ahead of schedule.  This article covers how to define scheduled start gates in update strategies, and how they complete during update run execution. -Important--Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager preview features are available on a self-service, opt-in basis. Previews are provided "as is" and "as available," and they're excluded from the service-level agreements and limited warranty. Azure Kubernetes Fleet Manager previews are partially covered by customer support on a best-effort basis. As such, these features aren't meant for production use.- ## Prerequisites  - Read the [conceptual overview of Fleet updates](concepts-update-orchestration), which provides an explanation of update runs, stages, groups, and strategies referenced in this guide.

The `kubectl describe pods` command shows repeated `FailedMount` events that have the `Aborted` status code instead of the `Internal` code that mount errors usually have:++```output+Events:+  Type     Reason       Age                   From     Message+  ----     ------       ----                  ----     -------+  Warning  FailedMount  22s (x10 over 4m32s)  kubelet  MountVolume.MountDevice failed for volume "<pv-name>" : rpc error: code = Aborted desc = An operation with the given Volume ID <volume-handle> already exists+```++The `<volume-handle>` value is the `volumeHandle` field of the PersistentVolume (PV).++### Cause++The Azure Files CSI driver allows only one operation at a time for each volume on a node. While the driver stages (mounts) or unstages a volume, it holds a lock for that volume. Kubelet retries failed or slow calls. If a retry reaches the driver while the first operation still holds the lock, the driver rejects the retry with the "An operation with the given Volume ID already exists" message.++The message itself doesn't identify the problem. It means that an earlier operation for the same volume on the same node didn't finish. The most common reasons are:++- **A slow or stuck mount operation.** The first mount takes longer than kubelet waits for a response. Examples are a stale or hung SMB connection to the storage account, intermittent network problems between the node and the storage account, or multiple leftover `cifs` mounts of the same share on the node.+- **A slow ownership change on an NFS share.** If the pod sets `fsGroup`, Kubernetes recursively changes ownership and permissions of the volume contents. On a share that has a large number of files, this operation can take a long time.+- **Two PVs that use the same `volumeHandle` on the same node.** Kubelet treats all PVs that have the same `volumeHandle` as one volume. Both pods share a single mount, so one pod might write to a different share than the one that its PV references.++### Troubleshooting++#### Step 1: Check whether the mount is still in progress or already exists++Use the `kubectl debug` command to open a shell on the node that hosts the pod, and then check for existing SMB mounts and connections:++```bash+kubectl debug node/<node-name> -it --image=mcr.microsoft.com/azurelinux/base/core:3.0 --profile=sysadmin -- chroot /host+```++```bash+mount | grep "type cifs"+ss -t | grep microsoft-ds+```++If the same share appears more than once, or if connections to the storage account are stuck, the node has a stale or duplicate mount.++#### Step 2: Check for duplicate volume handles++List the volume handle of every PV, and look for duplicate values:++```bash+kubectl get pv -o jsonpath='{range .items[?(@.spec.csi.driver=="file.csi.azure.com")]}{.spec.csi.volumeHandle}{"\t"}{.metadata.name}{"\n"}{end}' | sort+```++Each PV must have a unique `volumeHandle` value.++#### Step 3: Check the CSI driver logs on the node++Find the `csi-azurefile-node` pod that runs on the affected node, and look for the lock message and the original mount operation:++```bash+kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l app=csi-azurefile-node -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>+kubectl logs -n kube-system <csi-azurefile-node-pod-name> -c azurefile | grep -E "already exists|NodeStageVolume|timed out"+```++### Solution++1. If the operation is still running, wait for it to finish. Kubelet retries automatically, and the pod starts after the first operation completes.+2. If the operation doesn't finish, or the node has stale or duplicate mounts, delete the pod so that it's re-created. Then restart the CSI node pod on the same node:++    ```bash+    kubectl delete pod -n kube-system <csi-azurefile-node-pod-name>+    ```+3. If the problem persists or occurs again, [cordon and drain](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/) the node, and then let the pod be scheduled on a different node or on the same node after it's uncordoned. As a last resort, restart or reimage the node.+4. If two PVs have the same `volumeHandle`, give each PV a unique value. For a statically provisioned volume, use the `<resource-group>#<storage-account>#<file-share>` format:++    ```yaml+    csi:+      driver: file.csi.azure.com+      volumeHandle: <resource-group>#<storage-account>#<file-share>+    ```++    The `volumeHandle` field of an existing PV can't be changed. Delete and re-create the PV and PVC, and then re-create the pods.+5. If the volume is an NFS share that has many files and the pod sets `fsGroup`, set `fsGroupChangePolicy: OnRootMismatch` or `None` in the pod's `securityContext` to skip the recursive ownership change.+ ## `AuthorizationFailed` error during Azure Files share provisioning  ### Symptoms

AKS manages this label; don't set it manually to force a driver onto an unsupported OS. 3. To use Azure Managed Lustre with your cluster, ensure your Lustre workloads are scheduled on node pools running a supported OS (Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 or AzureLinux 3). Use [node selectors](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/#nodeselector) or [taints and tolerations](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/taint-and-toleration/) to constrain workloads to compatible nodes.++## Scenario 8: Uninstall is blocked by the volume guard++Driver v0.7.0 adds a default pre-delete guard for Helm-based removal and a volume check in the manifest cleanup script. A remaining PV blocks removal even when its workload is stopped and its file system is unmounted.++### Solution 8: Inspect the guard and complete safe cleanup++Capture the extension status if the resource still exists, Helm hook Job events, and guard logs before retrying. Failed Jobs expire and retries replace them. Use the installed release's namespace and labels, not an assumed `kube-system` namespace.++Follow the [blocked-uninstall reference](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/azurelustre-csi-driver/blob/v0.7.0/charts/README.md#troubleshoot-a-blocked-uninstall). Resolve remaining PVs through the safe retention and deletion procedure, or restore the guard's cluster-wide permission to list PVs if the inventory query fails. An API error isn't proof that no volumes remain. Don't use broad RBAC grants, remove Helm release secrets, or bypass hooks to clear the error.++For managed extensions, complete volume cleanup before requesting removal. The guard can't preserve an Azure extension resource that you already deleted while its Helm release is removed asynchronously. Also verify retained file systems separately; they remain billable. Replacing an earlier extension with v0.7.0 requires removal and reinstallation, not an in-place upgrade. Stop and contact Microsoft Support if a guarded installation blocks replacement while volumes must be preserved. Use the [managed-extension precautions](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/azurelustre-csi-driver/blob/v0.7.0/charts/README.md#azure-managed-extensions) and the removal path that matches how the extension was installed. For the preview AKS CLI enable option, use the separate [CLI lifecycle guide](/en-us/azure/aks/azure-managed-lustre-upgrade-uninstall-cli-preview).++If the Azure extension resource is gone but CSI pods remain, preserve their events and logs and contact Microsoft Support for recovery. Don't recreate the extension or run Helm directly against its remaining resources.

                                                                                                                                                        @@ -74,6 +74,28 @@ There's no automatic garbage collection of the FIC today when the last identity  Previously, workload identity required egress to `login.microsoftonline.com` so workloads could exchange service account tokens for Microsoft Entra access tokens. With identity bindings, token exchange requests route through a cluster-specific identity binding proxy operated by AKS. Direct egress to `login.microsoftonline.com` for token exchange isn't required. +### Why do my pods fail with `AADSTS700211` after I create the first identity binding on a cluster?++When you create the first identity binding on a cluster, AKS updates the workload identity webhook (`azure-wi-webhook-controller-manager` in the `kube-system` namespace) to support identity bindings. Until the updated webhook pods are running, the previous webhook mutates new pods. Those pods don't get the identity binding configuration and fall back to standard workload identity token exchange, which fails with `AADSTS700211` and names your cluster's OIDC issuer.++If your system node pool doesn't have enough spare CPU for an additional webhook pod, the new webhook pod stays in the `Pending` state and the update doesn't complete. The identity binding still shows a `Succeeded` provisioning state, because it doesn't track the webhook update.++To check the webhook pods and their events, run the following command:++```bash+kubectl describe pods --namespace kube-system --selector azure-workload-identity.io/system=true+```++If a pod is `Pending` and its events show `Insufficient cpu`, [scale your node pool](scale-cluster) or free up CPU on your system nodes. After the new webhook pods are running, delete and recreate your workload pods so the updated webhook mutates them.++### What happens if I delete and recreate a UAMI that identity bindings use?++A recreated UAMI gets a new client ID and principal ID. Existing identity bindings stay tied to the deleted identity, and updating them fails with a `ManagedIdentityRecreated` error. To use the new identity:++1. Delete and recreate each identity binding that references the UAMI. If another resource, such as a fleet, manages the binding, remove and reapply it through that resource.+2. Update your RBAC objects and service account annotations to the new client ID, and then restart your pods.+3. Assign Azure roles to the new principal ID.+ ### What limitations exist for identity bindings?  Identity bindings aren't yet supported on clusters configured with [API server virtual network integration](/en-us/azure/aks/api-server-vnet-integration).

Replace the resource ID, VM size, and zone with values for your reservation.++```yaml+    apiVersion: karpenter.azure.com/v1beta1+    kind: AKSNodeClass+    metadata:+      name: reserved+    spec:+      capacityReservation:+        groupID: /subscriptions/<subscription-id>/resourceGroups/<crg-resource-group>/providers/Microsoft.Compute/capacityReservationGroups/<crg-name>+```++For a regional, zone-less member, replace the `topology.kubernetes.io/zone` requirement with:++```yaml+- key: karpenter.azure.com/placement-scope+  operator: In+  values: ["regional"]+```++Important++The association is a launch constraint, not a preference: every node you launch from this class targets the group.
